The two papers reach opposite headline verdicts on answer quality, and both attribute the disagreement to the wiki arm's serving/context-selection strategy rather than to the wiki representation itself.

The conflict: the preregistered agent-browsed comparison (24 papers, 13 questions) does not crown a winner — the wiki's organization advantage fell below the registered +2.0 threshold (+1.625 judge-averaged on structural_integrity), point-source groundedness parity was fragile (+0.667 judge-averaged, P(mu>=0)=0.660), and on corrected claim-level scoring RAG's cited claims were supported 53.8% versus 41.5% for the wiki [2605.18490#s26.p2][2605.18490#s27.p3][2605.18490#s37.p6]. The classroom comparison (59 questions) instead finds the compiled wiki clearly ahead overall (9.95 vs 9.05 of 10; grounded 98% vs 81%) and even on topic-page questions (9.96 vs 9.33), with the advantage roughly tripling on cross-page questions [2609.25303#s16.p2][2609.25303#s16.p5][2609.25303#s16.p6].

The key factor: the classroom authors attribute the difference partly to their wiki arm having no context-selection step that can fail, reading their result as the gap between real retrieval and perfect context selection, and treating it as directional rather than general [2609.25303#s24.p3]. The concept page frames the same point as serving strategy: a tool-using agent pays for its own traversal (up to 30 turns), reversing the cost direction relative to a wiki served as retrieved pages [2605.18490#s8.p1]. Relatedly, the agent-browsed study's decomposition-retrieval RAG variant closed about 94% of the synthesis gap at 491k query tokens versus 1,651k for the wiki, showing the baseline's retrieval strategy also drives the verdict [2605.18490#s44.p2][2605.18490#s44.p4].
